Concretely, this was observed in pruning experiments on LLaMA-class models where heads identified as low-importance by Taylor pruning were disproportionately the ones handling sink routing, and the failure only became visible beyond 4K tokens. The expert-level implication is that any compression scheme evaluated only on short-context benchmarks will systematically underestimate damage to sink geometry, because short contexts don't stress-test the attention normalization stability that sinks provide.

Models trained with explicit attention entropy regularization do appear to develop weaker positional sinks, but they don't eliminate the underlying problem — they displace it. Mixture-of-experts models add another dimension: because different experts see different token subsets, sink formation becomes expert-local, and Mixtral-class architectures show that individual experts can develop strong internal sinks on their routed tokens while the global attention picture looks more diffuse — this means KV eviction policies operating on global attention scores will systematically underestimate the importance of tokens that are high-value sinks within a specific expert's routing but low-salience globally. The interaction with KV eviction is thus inverted from the standard case: for dense models, the danger is evicting the sink and causing collapse; for entropy-regularized or sparse models, the danger is that the eviction budget calculation is wrong because there's no obvious high-importance token to protect, so policies like H2O (Heavy Hitter Oracle, Zhang et al. 2023) that use cumulative attention scores to identify important tokens will spread their "protect" budget across many marginal tokens instead of concentrating it correctly. The practical implication is that KV eviction policies are not architecture-agnostic and need to be co-designed with the attention training objective — a policy tuned on LLaMA will likely over-evict on entropy-regularized models and under-protect on models with strong delimiter sinks from instruction tuning.

Prefill importance scores are a surprisingly unreliable predictor of decode-phase importance, and the failure mode is asymmetric: tokens that look important during prefill mostly stay important during decode, but a significant fraction of decode-critical tokens score low during prefill, making prefill-based eviction a one-way trap where evicted tokens cannot be recovered. The core reason is that prefill computes attention over the entire prompt in parallel, so each token's score reflects its importance for understanding the prompt, while decode attention reflects importance for generating the next token given partial output — these are related but distinct computational tasks, and for question-answering or instruction-following tasks, the answer-relevant spans of the prompt often receive moderate prefill attention (they're contextually present but not yet "activated" by the generative process) and then spike in importance once decoding begins to reference them. Concretely, SnapKV (Li et al., 2024) addressed this by observing that the last few tokens of the prompt — the query region — provide a better signal for decode-phase importance than full-prefill cumulative scores, because those final tokens are closest in distribution to the decode queries that will follow; their experiments on LongBench showed that prefill scores from the query region alone matched or exceeded full-prefill scores for predicting which KV entries mattered during generation. The prefill/decode mismatch is worst for retrieval-heavy tasks like multi-hop reasoning or document QA, where the model must return to specific evidence spans mid-generation that weren't heavily attended during the initial read-through — these spans are prime eviction candidates under naïve H2O but are exactly what the decode phase needs. A further complication is that decode attention patterns shift within the decode phase itself: early decode tokens often attend broadly for context-setting while late decode tokens attend narrowly to recently generated content and specific evidence anchors, meaning a single static eviction decision made at prefill-end is trying to serve a non-stationary decode attention distribution. This argues for online eviction policies that continue updating importance estimates during decode, but these carry their own cost — the overhead of re-scoring and potentially re-evicting mid-generation adds latency that partially defeats the purpose of KV compression in the first place.
